title: One-dimensional kinetic shocks: BGK/Shakhov PINNs and DVM
subtitle: FlowMLLab Week 10.2 | English lecture notes | Ehsan Roohi

paper.title: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for kinetic shock waves: simultaneous accuracy of lower- and higher-order moments, with and without moment supervision

pages.title: The question: can correct bulk fields hide an incorrect distribution?

blocks.text: A kinetic model describes how molecules populate velocity space. Density, velocity and temperature are only a few integrals of that distribution. Two predictions can agree on these bulk fields and disagree strongly on heat flux, stress or fourth-order moments. This lecture asks how to detect that disagreement, and what can be concluded from a physics-informed neural network (PINN) when its available numerical reference also changes under refinement.

blocks.caption: One physical coordinate and three molecular velocity coordinates. BGK and Shakhov are alternative collision models; a discrete-velocity method (DVM) and a PINN are numerical approaches to a specified model. Match the model, case, units, time and reference.

blocks.text: The companion notebook combines fresh CPU quadrature experiments, retained research shock predictions and a new PINN trained from random initialization. Tables A–G identify the retained cases, check jumps and moment information, audit quadrature and compare research profiles. The added training section fits a small BGK model and compares its reconstructed physical fields with a separately computed DVM reference.

Weeks 3 and 8 supply kinetic moments and gas-dynamic jumps. Week 10 supplies the habit of tracing a prediction to its dataset. This unit adds deterministic kinetic equations and distribution-level neural approximation; the existing DSMC lessons remain separate.

pages.title: One-dimensional flow still has three velocity dimensions

blocks.text: The physical position is x and time is t. The molecular velocity is the three-component vector v. The mean flow points along x, while molecules retain transverse motion. Eliminating transverse energy would change the gas model. Throughout this lecture the variables are nondimensional, the gas is monatomic, and its heat-capacity ratio is 5/3.

blocks.explanation: The peculiar velocity c measures molecular motion relative to the local mean; e is the squared peculiar speed, not the specific internal energy.

blocks.latex: \rho=\int f\,\mathrm{d}^3v,\quad \rho u=\int v_x f\,\mathrm{d}^3v,\quad 3\rho T=\int e f\,\mathrm{d}^3v
blocks.explanation: All velocity integrals refer to the complete three-dimensional velocity domain unless a numerical truncation is stated.
The nondimensional gas constant is one. The equilibrium internal energy per unit mass is 3T/2.
The Maxwellian uses the density, mean velocity and temperature of f, computed consistently with the same quadrature.

blocks.text: A distribution has units and a normalization convention even after nondimensionalization. The source uses p = ρT; importing a dimensional pressure or a temperature with a different thermal-speed scaling would silently change the target. Table A records the normalization and collision model before any error is calculated.

Integrate a Maxwellian as a first test. Recover its prescribed density, velocity and temperature, then confirm that central deviatoric stress, heat flux and the higher nonequilibrium moments vanish. A finite velocity grid approaches these identities with quadrature and domain refinement.

pages.title: BGK and Shakhov describe different relaxation physics

blocks.explanation: Transport is shared by both models. The target distribution and relaxation time define the collision model.
BGK relaxes toward the local Maxwellian and has model Prandtl number Pr = 1.
The Shakhov correction changes the heat-flux relaxation rate. The monatomic Shakhov cases use Pr = 2/3.

rows: Transient BGK and Shakhov tube cases

blocks.text: These are three declared case settings, not interchangeable definitions of τ. A change from constant relaxation time to 1/ρ changes the spatial collision scale. Comparing solutions with different τ laws would mix modeling and numerical error.

The Shakhov target is a Maxwellian multiplied by a polynomial correction. It can be negative in velocity tails when q is nonzero. Record this behavior; do not silently clip negative target values. Clipping changes the collision moments and can destroy the intended conservation and heat-relaxation identities.

At Pr = 1 the Shakhov correction vanishes, giving a direct check against BGK. At equilibrium q = 0, both targets reduce to the same Maxwellian. These identities support a small CPU exercise independent of neural shock training.

pages.title: Reduced distributions: retain the transverse information you need

blocks.text: For planar flow, transverse velocity integrals can be represented by three functions of x, t and the remaining velocity v = vx. Let r2 = vy2 + vz2. The definitions below have no factor of one half in h.

blocks.latex: g=\int f\,\mathrm{d}v_y\mathrm{d}v_z,\quad h=\int r^2f\,\mathrm{d}v_y\mathrm{d}v_z,\quad k=\int r^4f\,\mathrm{d}v_y\mathrm{d}v_z
blocks.explanation: g retains mass, h retains the transverse second moment, and k retains transverse fourth-order information.

blocks.caption: Moment dependency map. The g and h reductions determine bulk fields, heat flux, normal stress, the selected third moment and the combined fourth-order diagnostic S. Separate R and Δ additionally require k.

blocks.explanation: Here c = v − u. These Maxwellian reductions integrate the transverse velocity plane to infinity.

blocks.text: Knowing g and h does not generally determine k. Setting k = 8T<super>2</super>g would impose an additional transverse-Maxwellian assumption, not recover information from g and h. Table C constructs two positive distributions that expose the distinction.

The analytic infinite-domain reductions differ from the finite rectangular transverse sums used in the transient implementation. Preserve the source quadrature when reproducing a saved result; a change of integration domain is a numerical experiment that must be identified.

pages.title: Signed central moments and reduced Shakhov targets

blocks.explanation: Recover the mean first; central moments must use the same u in every integrand.
σ uses the kinetic central-moment sign convention and can have either sign. The Cauchy viscous-stress convention reverses that sign. Positive q denotes heat flux in the positive x direction.
m denotes m<sub>xxx</sub> = ∫[c<sub>x</sub><super>3</super> − (3/5)c<sub>x</sub> e]f d<super>3</super>v; it is not simply the raw third moment.

blocks.text: For infinite transverse integration, define A and use it to reduce the Shakhov target. The transverse-energy target is not a simple multiple of the mass target.

blocks.explanation: A depends on the remaining velocity through c.
The mass reduction has the constant −3 in its correction.
The h and k constants are respectively −1 and +1, from transverse Gaussian moment integration.

blocks.text: A sign error in σ can be hidden by plotting absolute values. A missing factor in h alters temperature and heat flux. The notebook therefore reports signed profiles and checks moment definitions before interpreting a model ranking.

pages.title: Fourth-order moments and a positive counterexample

blocks.explanation: R removes the equilibrium-coupled deviatoric contribution.
Δ measures the excess contracted fourth moment. R and Δ vanish for a Maxwellian.
The k terms cancel in S. Agreement in S does not establish separate agreement in R and Δ.

blocks.text: Construct g as a standard normal distribution. In case A use a transverse two-dimensional Gaussian with temperature 1. In case B use an equal mixture of transverse Gaussians with temperatures 0.5 and 1.5. Both complete distributions are positive and their transverse means are zero.

Table C must recover this result by integration. It is a derived teaching counterexample, not a saved shock simulation. It proves that g and h alone do not identify both fourth-order moments. Adding two target names to a report cannot restore missing distributional information.

pages.title: Stationary shocks: jumps, incoming states and conserved fluxes

blocks.text: For a steady normal shock, upstream density and temperature equal one. The upstream Mach number M determines the equilibrium states through the monatomic Rankine–Hugoniot relations.

blocks.explanation: The downstream density follows from conservation across the shock.
The end states do not specify the internal kinetic structure or shock thickness.
Mass and momentum fluxes are spatially constant in the steady problem.
The energy flux contains signed stress-work and heat-flux terms.

blocks.text: Table B recomputes these targets. Report each profile flux defect as J/J<sub>target</sub> − 1, or multiply by 100 when explicitly reporting percent. Small flux defects are necessary consistency evidence. They do not establish agreement of the complete velocity distribution or its higher moments with DVM.

Incoming populations use the appropriate far-field equilibrium: positive velocities enter from the left and negative velocities from the right. This velocity-dependent condition differs from prescribing all populations at both ends.

pages.title: The transient tube is a different experiment

blocks.text: The transient cases start from a smooth local-Maxwellian transition on x in [−0.5, 0.5]. Both sides initially have zero mean velocity. This is not a stationary shock initialized at Rankine–Hugoniot end states.

blocks.explanation: H selects the right-hand state through a smooth transition.
The initial distribution is the Maxwellian associated with these local fields.

blocks.text: The source uses constant τ = Kn = 1 and final time t = 0.02. Inflow is prescribed only for velocities entering the domain. Transient quadrature uses 48 × 20 × 20 uniform rectangular velocity nodes in [−7, 7]<super>3</super>, distinct from the Gauss–Legendre teaching experiment in Table D.

blocks.explanation: The invariants give a time-dependent conservation law. Spatially constant flux is not the correct transient test.
A transient finite-volume check balances the change of integrated U against boundary flux over a time interval.

blocks.text: The elapsed time is only 0.02 relaxation times. The characteristic collision-source weight is at most 1 − exp(−0.02) = 0.0198013. Transport dominates this short experiment. Nearly coincident BGK and Shakhov profiles do not establish equivalent collision models.

The retained DVM uses upwind transport with frozen exponential relaxation and CFL 0.4. Source comparisons include 1600/3200 spatial references and a later 6400-cell BGK reference. Grid identity is part of every Table E or G comparison.

pages.title: The transient network predicts the collision source

blocks.text: The transient PINN takes normalized inputs (t/tf, 2x), uses two 32-unit tanh hidden layers, and outputs raw quantities rρ, ru, rT, plus rq for Shakhov. It does not directly output f, g or h. The source fields use the initial profiles ρ₀(x), T₀(x) and the time factor a.

blocks.latex: a=t/t_f,\quad \rho_\theta=\rho_0e^{a r_\rho/2},\quad u_\theta=a r_u,\quad T_\theta=T_0e^{a r_T/2}
blocks.explanation: This lifting preserves the initial macroscopic fields; the density and temperature source fields are positive.
The additional Shakhov output supplies the target heat flux. BGK does not need this output.
Along x(s) = x − v<sub>x</sub>(t − s), ℓ ends at the initial plane or the incoming boundary. The source integral uses 16 Gauss–Legendre time nodes.

blocks.text: The loss matches moments integrated from reconstructed f to the source network moments: density, streamwise momentum and energy, with heat-flux consistency added for Shakhov. Reported endpoint observables are integrated from f; they are not simply the source network outputs.

The stationary M2 construction is different: a three-layer, 64-unit tanh network uses scaled position, a localized position feature, streamwise velocity, transverse squared speed and a prescribed blend s(x). Its bounded scalar correction modifies B = (1 − s)M₁ + sM₂. B is positive, but the signed multiplicative correction does not guarantee a nonnegative distribution.
These representation choices explain why a small moment-consistency loss can coexist with distributional defects. Preserve the actual source architecture when interpreting its gates.

pages.title: Loss functions and the roles of reference data

blocks.explanation: A direct distribution PINN can use this differential residual, with automatic differentiation. A steady residual omits the time derivative; the transient source instead uses characteristic reconstruction and moment consistency.
Schematic terms: equation residual, initial/incoming boundaries, moment consistency and optional data supervision. Actual source stages retain their declared terms and weights.
Every supervised moment has locations, targets, a scale s<sub>a</sub> and a count N<sub>a</sub>. Loss magnitude depends on these choices.

blocks.text: Equation-trained means DVM targets are not fitting observations for that construction; it does not erase reference comparisons made during research. Data-assisted means numerical moment observations enter fitting. Those same observations cannot then be presented as independent validation.

Five-field S0 supervises ρ, u, T, q and σ. The later eight-moment construction adds m, R and Δ. S is a derived ninth diagnostic. The final source records 160 observations for each bulk field and 42 for each of the five remaining moments: 690 observations. Its higher-moment window is [−0.104, 0.134].

Reference-derived scales and some full-profile acceptance guards also use reference information. Excluding observation-bracketing nodes reduces direct reuse, but neighboring numerical samples remain correlated. Tables A and G therefore record fitting, guard access and assessment separately.

pages.title: Optimization stages are trajectories, not a controlled ranking

blocks.text: A smaller final loss can result from additional updates, changed collocation points, changed quadrature, changed objectives or a better optimizer. Isolating an optimizer effect requires holding these other factors fixed and matching a declared compute budget. The retained stationary M2 sequence does not meet that design.

rows: Earlier checkpoint of each seed trajectory
Further continuation with changed sampling/quadrature and incoming gate

blocks.text: Table F retains source seeds 141001, 141002 and 141003. Evaluate each seed before averaging errors. The error of an averaged profile differs from the mean of individual errors because cancellations can reduce the former.
Mean heat-flux error can improve while mean stress error worsens. Both belong in the conclusion. Avoid selecting the best-looking seed or reporting only the field that benefits from the final stage.

The final M2 records pass flux, phase, quadrature and positive-macroscopic-field checks. All three nevertheless fail the projection and tail gates; two fail the kinetic gate. Several necessary physical checks do not establish complete acceptance.

Characteristic repair is a separate intervention. In the paper’s M7 example, two deterministic characteristic updates improve an existing neural field without updating its weights. This demonstrates a hybrid correction, not additional neural training or an optimizer win.

Retained research cost and newly measured CPU teaching cost describe different computations. The new training section records its own work and stop reason; a short classroom run does not establish a research-scale speedup.

pages.title: Measure errors on declared grids and retain their signs

blocks.explanation: An unweighted percent relative L2 on the stated samples. It reproduces a source metric only when the source uses this convention; the notebook teaching rescore instead uses the spatial integral below.
Tables E–G approximate both spatial integrals with trapezoidal weights on the declared common grid. Table G uses 399 common-overlap nodes without extrapolation.
Signed pointwise error locates improvement and deterioration; a norm alone cannot show their positions.

blocks.text: For a moment that crosses zero, pointwise reference division creates artificial singularities. Use a declared global norm or physical amplitude for normalized errors and retain the physical signed profile. A small global norm can coexist with a wrong sign in a small-amplitude tail.

Compare arrays on their actual shared support. If interpolation is required, identify which field is interpolated, onto which grid and over what overlap. Do not extrapolate outside the supplied domain and call the result measured coverage. The notebook common-overlap rescore is distinguished from the paper’s published assessment grid.

Stationary shocks have a translational phase. A midpoint shift may remove location error, but changes the question. Report unshifted error and the shift before interpreting a centered comparison. A shift selected using the assessment reference uses target information.

blocks.explanation: One explicit teaching thickness diagnostic. Declare the derivative estimate, grid, end states and units; this is not an automatically adopted paper metric.

blocks.text: Thickness is sensitive to mesh and differentiation. A grid study holds model, domain, time and comparison definition fixed. Changing reference families as well as resolution does not isolate discretization error. This distinction matters when model error and reference-refinement differences have similar magnitudes.

pages.title: A fresh CPU audit of homogeneous collision physics

blocks.text: Table D integrates a positive mixture of three-dimensional Maxwellians. It checks the collision model with controllable velocity quadrature without solving a new spatial shock. The exact infinite-domain mixture has ρ = 1, u = 0.2, T = 1.19, σ = 0.56 and q = −1.071.

blocks.explanation: Arguments are density, streamwise mean velocity and temperature. Each component has zero transverse mean.
At homogeneous constant macroscopic state, stress relaxes at rate 1/τ and heat flux at rate Pr/τ.

blocks.caption: Analytic homogeneous relaxation, with model and normalization indicated. Table D supplies fresh quadrature checks of initial rates and invariant integrals. These curves are not new spatial shock predictions.

blocks.text: At one relaxation time, σ/σ<sub>0</sub> = 0.367879 for both models. For q/q<sub>0</sub> the values are 0.367879 for BGK and 0.513417 for Shakhov. Negative initial q approaches zero from below, so its initial derivative is positive.
Inspect the minimum Shakhov target and conserved collision moments as well as the rates. This distinguishes tail positivity from quadrature error and explains why clipping is not a neutral repair.

pages.title: Numerical investigations 1–3: exact targets before shocks

blocks.text: Preliminary reading — Table A. Classify each case by stationary/transient, BGK/Shakhov and equation-trained/data-assisted. Check source commit, τ law, reference grid and data role. Preserve unknown entries. This registry reading supports the seven investigations below.

items: Investigation 1 — Table B. Set M = 2, γ = 5/3. Recover ρ₂ = 2.2857142857, u₂ = 1.1296201426, T₂ = 2.078125 and JE = 15.0616019019. Check all fluxes at both end states. Then omit uσ from the energy flux of one retained M2 profile. Compare the internal defect and explain why equilibrium jump checks alone miss this omission.

Investigation 2 — Table C. Integrate the positive constructions on page 6. Report ρ, u, T, h/g, k/g, σ, q, m, R, Δ and S. Identical g and h must yield (R, Δ) = (0, 0) and (−2/3, 2), with S = 0 in both.

Investigation 3 — Table D. Use the page-13 mixture, τ = 1, Gauss–Legendre orders [12, 20, 32], cutoffs [4, 6, 8] and Pr in [1, 2/3]: 18 combinations on [−V, V]3. Report computed moments, invariant integrals, stress/heat rates, target minimum and deviations from analytic values.

blocks.text: Interpretation 1. At fixed cutoff, does increasing order eliminate truncation error? Support your answer with two rows.
Interpretation 2. If clipping removes a negative target tail, which conservation or relaxation integral changes? Decide whether the altered operator remains the declared Shakhov model.

pages.title: Transient BGK: similar profiles can conceal a mixed change

blocks.caption: Transient BGK at t = 0.02 and constant τ = 1. Retained PINN predictions and the identified matched DVM reference are compared on their actual common support. The legend identifies methods and references.

blocks.text: The paper’s 100-to-300-SSB continuation comparison against the same 3200-cell reference reduces heat-flux error from 0.410617% to 0.410026%. Stress error increases from 0.356950% to 0.360440%. The small changes have different directions.

Table E recomputes each retained available field: ρ, u, T, q, σ, m, R, Δ and derived S. State the reference and samples beside the values. Do not combine the 3200-cell continuation statement with a later 6400-cell assessment as though only the network changed.

First locate the transition, extrema and zero crossings. Then inspect where the prediction departs from the reference. Tiny global bulk-field errors cannot substitute for heat-flux or higher-moment assessment.
This short-time case mainly tests characteristic transport with a small collision contribution. The homogeneous audit more clearly exhibits the BGK heat-relaxation rate.

pages.title: Transient Shakhov: match the model before comparing methods

blocks.caption: Transient Shakhov at t = 0.02, Pr = 2/3 and constant τ = 1. The DVM solves the same Shakhov model. This page has its own model-matched comparison.

blocks.text: Against the same 3200-cell Shakhov reference, extending 100 to 300 SSB updates reduces q error from 0.412103% to 0.410056%, while σ error increases from 0.356831% to 0.360561%. Additional updates do not guarantee simultaneous improvement of all observables.

The collision-source weight is below 0.02 at this final time, so differences from the preceding BGK page can be subtle. That agrees with the short timescale; it does not remove the Prandtl-number distinction.

Table E keeps model labels separate. Compare signed q, σ and available higher moments against the Shakhov DVM on the declared overlap. Leave a missing source moment unavailable rather than deriving it from an assumed transverse Maxwellian.

Table D connects this evidence with collision physics: at identical macroscopic state Shakhov relaxes q more slowly than BGK while their stress rates agree. Transport and the evolving local state make the spatial problem richer than that homogeneous identity.

pages.title: Stationary Mach 2: three seeds and incomplete physical acceptance

blocks.caption: Stationary Shakhov Mach 2, illustrated with seed 141001. The curves compare its Adam, SSB and split-half stages with matched DVM. The table below reports the mean of all three individual-seed errors. The last continuation changes accumulated computation and aspects of the numerical objective.

blocks.text: These paper-reported values are means of three individual-seed errors, not the error of an ensemble-mean profile. The final continuation improves mean q but worsens mean σ. Table F retains seed rows to reveal whether this tradeoff is consistent across trajectories.

All three final runs fail projection and tail gates; two also fail the kinetic gate. Flux, phase, quadrature and positive-macroscopic-field checks pass. The evidence supports a substantial but incomplete improvement under a staged workflow, not a successful all-gates solve or an isolated optimizer ranking.

pages.title: Supervision: identify S0, eight moments and equation training

blocks.caption: BGK teaching common-overlap rescore against the 6400-cell reference, without extrapolation. Legends distinguish equation-trained, five-field supervised S0 and final eight-moment data-assisted profiles. S0 comes from the stage0 export; model170 is a different eight-moment source object.

blocks.text: The five-field S0 values below are the paper’s full 6400-reference assessment: q/σ errors are 2.8759%/3.0891%, while m/R/Δ errors are 105.88%/141.09%/138.64%. Its fourth-order profiles can have the wrong core sign. The final-versus-equation examples below instead use the paper’s 401-node matched grid. Table G independently rescores all three methods on 399 common-overlap nodes with trapezoidal weights.

The final eight-moment data-assisted result reduces those failures, but q, σ, m, R and Δ remain less accurate than the equation-trained result on that matched reference. Better bulk-field errors do not establish uniform improvement.

For example, final data-assisted versus equation-trained paper errors are 0.3306% versus 0.2051% in q, 0.6654% versus 0.1806% in σ, and 1.9655% versus 0.8535% in R. Table G includes all fields and source flags. The comparison describes retained constructions; it does not isolate supervision as a causal effect under equal budgets.

pages.title: Read failures, refinements and repairs as part of the result

items: Reference sensitivity. The paper-reported 3200-to-6400 BGK difference is about 0.2048% for q, 0.1802% for σ and 0.8511% for R. Equation-trained errors against 6400 have similar magnitudes. This limits inference about error against an unknown continuum-in-space solution.

Supervised acceptance. The final eight-moment record retains paper_admission = false and all_criteria_pass = false. It used 35 updates in 40 attempts and stopped at the attempt cap. The physical E4 audit at 64 separately declared points and E8 at 64 unused points added after first assessment failed the 0.1% tolerance.

Small tails matter. The final data-assisted source reports a wrong stress sign for x < −0.23 and wrong R/Δ signs for x > 0.19 at amplitudes below 0.5% of their extrema. A global norm does not certify every local sign.

Characteristic repair. For stationary BGK M7, two characteristic updates reduce q/σ errors from 3.36838%/1.34126% to 0.41606%/0.43422%, with zero neural-weight updates. A boundary residual nevertheless increases. This is a hybrid correction with multiple diagnostics.

Domain and reference. M8 has a small core stress error after repair but 1.6681% on the full overlap. M12 error values vary with reference family; those comparisons are not a controlled grid-refinement sequence.

blocks.text: A defensible result states its model, domain, reference, observable, intervention and failed checks. Acknowledge useful improvement without converting it into a stronger claim than the evidence supports. These reported examples are reading evidence; the notebook does not regenerate M7, M8 or M12 shocks.

pages.title: Investigations 4–7 and a reproducible scientific claim

items: Investigation 4 — Table E. For each transient model, report signed q and σ errors and the stated global norm on the declared common samples. Identify a continuation improvement and a deterioration. Explain why constant spatial energy flux is inappropriate at t = 0.02.

Investigation 5 — Table F. Compute each of the three seed errors at every stage, then their mean. Identify the heat-flux gain and stress regression. Distinguish mean individual errors from error of an averaged profile, and retain failed gates and optimization confounders.

Investigation 6 — Density thickness. Choose one M2 stage and its matched DVM. Subsample each retained density profile at strides 1, 2 and 4 over the common interval. Record sample counts, derivative convention, maximum density slope and δρ. Explain differences as sampling/differentiation sensitivity: these are not new CFD solutions or a solver mesh-refinement study.

Investigation 7 — Table G. Compare equation-trained, five-field S0 and final eight-moment BGK against the identified reference. Report eight moments plus derived S, global errors and signed tails. Audit observation/guard access, reference refinement and final admission flags. Write a short claim separating fresh CPU diagnostics from retained predictions.

pages.title: Train a kinetic PINN from random initialization

blocks.text: The added exercise trains a new neural model on the CPU. It loads no saved research weights. The physical case is the transient BGK tube already defined on page 8: τ = 1 and t<sub>f</sub> = 0.02. The initial condition is a single local Maxwellian built from the smooth density and temperature profiles, not a mixture of the left and right Maxwellians.

The network takes normalized time and position and predicts the density, streamwise velocity and temperature of a collision source. Positive density and temperature lifting follow the construction on page 9. The trained observables are then integrated from the characteristic reconstruction. A source-network temperature and the temperature of its reconstructed distribution are distinct quantities until self-consistency is satisfied.

rows: 2 tanh hidden layers, width 24; 747 parameters; seed 1729
adam, lbfgs or adam_lbfgs; default 100 Adam + 20 L-BFGS outer steps
64 fixed points; a separate frozen audit set

blocks.text: The notebook builds a PINNConfig, calls train and evaluates the initial and trained states with evaluate. Freeze the configuration before comparison, train and freeze the weights, then evaluate against DVM. DVM fields do not enter the objective or determine the default settings. An inspected benchmark used to revise choices is no longer an untouched blind assessment.
This is a fresh teaching computation with its own discretization and budget. It is not a rerun of the full historical training campaign or a newly trained Shakhov network.

pages.title: Characteristics build transport, initial data and inflow into the model

blocks.explanation: The learned source fields define a one-dimensional Maxwellian reduction at each point on a molecular trajectory.
The three components are the BGK source reductions for g, h and k. Transverse Gaussian integration is analytic over the infinite transverse plane.
Here z = (g,h,k), and the source is sampled at x(s) = x − v(t − s). Positive Gauss–Legendre time weights approximate the source integral.

blocks.text: Trace backward to the first initial-plane or incoming-boundary intersection. Positive velocities can reach the left reservoir; negative velocities can reach the right reservoir. A zero velocity reaches the initial plane. The reservoir supplies the exact incoming Maxwellian reductions. Outgoing populations are not overwritten with prescribed boundary macroscopic fields.

Initial and inflow data are enforced at the distribution level. Their numerical moments still have finite velocity-quadrature error. Do not claim that hard distribution data make all discrete moments exact.

This is a neural integral-equation PINN: self-consistency makes the learned Maxwellian source a source for the nonlinear BGK equation. Autograd differentiates through the quadrature with respect to network weights; no time or position derivatives are needed in this training objective.

Reconstruct k along the same characteristics. Setting k = 8T<super>2</super>g using the final reconstructed temperature would impose a false transverse closure on a mixture of contributions with different source temperatures. All nine reported observables come from reconstructed g, h and k.

pages.title: The loss learns a self-consistent collision source

blocks.text: At a collocation point, reconstruct g and h by characteristic integration and evaluate their axial velocity quadrature. Compare the resulting conserved moments with the moments of the network source. The residuals below use quadrature weights w<sub>j</sub> and fixed upstream scales.

blocks.explanation: The density residual compares the source with reconstructed mass.
The momentum residual uses momentum, not a separately fitted velocity label.
The total-energy residual includes longitudinal and transverse kinetic energy. The three upstream scales are all one in this nondimensional case.
The brackets denote an average over the fixed collocation set; the three nonnegative weights are student controls.

blocks.text: The 64 seeded points put half the positions in the central interval [−0.15, 0.15] and half across [−0.5, 0.5]. One quarter of times equal t<sub>f</sub>; the rest stratify the open time interval. Points remain fixed. The loss uses no DVM normalization, time division or supervised moment labels. Initial and incoming data enter through reconstruction, not penalty terms.

Record the three unweighted component losses as well as the weighted sum. A zero weight is an ablation that omits one consistency equation, not complete BGK closure. Increasing a weight can reduce its residual while another component or a derived heat-flux/stress profile deteriorates. Weight changes also alter optimization scales; a smaller weighted total alone is not a fair accuracy ranking.

Evaluate the frozen model on a separate final-time grid and inspect reconstructed moments. A small training residual is neither a guarantee of small higher-moment error nor proof that the velocity and time quadratures are resolved.

pages.title: Adam, L-BFGS and a controlled hybrid comparison

blocks.explanation: Adam keeps moving estimates of the gradient and its elementwise square; g<sub>k</sub> is the gradient of the weighted physics loss.
The hats divide the moving estimates by 1 − β<sub>1</sub><super>k</super> and 1 − β<sub>2</sub><super>k</super>, respectively. The learning rate η controls the update scale.
L-BFGS approximates inverse-curvature action from recent parameter and gradient changes; it does not form the full dense Hessian.

blocks.text: A strong-Wolfe search requires sufficient decrease relative to the initial directional derivative, and bounds the magnitude of the new directional derivative by a chosen fraction of its initial magnitude. It may test several step lengths. Each closure must use identical collocation points, quadrature and weights: resampling changes the objective being searched.

The hybrid performs Adam and then L-BFGS on the fixed objective. It is not automatically more accurate or cheaper. Compare initialized copies of the same architecture with the same seed and points; record completed outer updates, closure evaluations, elapsed time and stop reason. A completed L-BFGS call can have zero parameter change or require several gradient evaluations.

For depth or width experiments, record the changed parameter count. The same random seed across different architectures is reproducible initialization, not identical starting weights. Compare more than one seed before asserting a robust capacity effect.

Keep the physical case and reference access fixed. A step cap or elapsed-time stop is a budget outcome, not evidence of convergence. In this short-time problem, hardwired transport can already give accurate initial profiles; compare both the initialized and trained predictions.

pages.title: An independent finite-volume BGK reference

blocks.text: The new NumPy DVM evolves g, h and k on uniform physical cells at each axial velocity. The notebook uses 400 and 800 cells with 48 Gauss–Legendre velocity nodes on [−7, 7], plus an 800-cell, 64-node check. Analytic transverse integration matches the fresh PINN; the paper’s finite rectangular velocity reference remains separately labelled.

blocks.explanation: Here z = (g,h,k). The finite-volume operator combines face transport with a local Maxwellian relaxation source.

blocks.text: MUSCL reconstruction uses minmod slopes: keep the smaller magnitude and common sign when neighboring differences have the same sign; otherwise use zero slope. Upwind flux selects the left face state for positive velocity and the right state for negative velocity. Incoming boundary faces receive reservoir Maxwellians; outgoing populations use interior data.

Recompute density, velocity, temperature and all three Maxwellian reductions at both stages. Freezing the first-stage target changes this algorithm.
The implementation uses a combined transport/collision restriction and shortens the step to end exactly at the requested final time.

pages.title: Read the initial, trained and DVM profiles together

blocks.caption: Fresh CPU BGK baseline: seed 1729, depth 2, width 24, t = 0.02. Compare initial and trained reconstructed moments with the independent 800-cell DVM at its cell centers, using 48 axial nodes and PINN time order 12. Table H reports nine fields.

blocks.text: The collision weight is at most 1 − exp(−0.02) = 0.0198013. Much short-time transport is already prescribed, so retain the initialized baseline.

The measured training loss fell from 0.003030 to 0.0008090, and the unused physics-audit loss from 0.003488 to 0.0009058. Relative L<sub>2</sub> errors improved for heat flux (0.3011 → 0.2364%) and stress (0.9829 → 0.5510%), while velocity (1.0029 → 1.3684%) and temperature (0.01297 → 0.01342%) worsened.

Table I tests DVM 400-to-800 cells, DVM velocity order 48-to-64, and frozen-PINN quadrature 48 × 12 to 64 × 16. The fixed-CFL spatial/time changes are 0.1213% for heat flux and 0.1374% for stress. These are sensitivity measures, not uncertainty bounds; this check alone does not establish that small training gains are numerically resolved. Restrict finer DVM distributions before forming coarse-cell moments.

Table J retains all seven predeclared configurations. Depth 3 gave heat-flux/stress errors of 0.1095%/0.1746%, but the two-layer baseline remains the default declared before DVM scoring. One seed and unequal work do not establish a generally best architecture or optimizer.

pages.title: Five further investigations: train, measure and interpret

blocks.text: Continue the original seven investigations with tasks 8–12. State which results you freshly generated and which published runs you inspected. Preserve the physical case, initial and final states, configurations, seeds, hashes, work counts and stop reasons.

items: 8. Depth — Tables H/J. Train depths 1, 2 and 3 at width 24 with seed 1729 and the same physics points. Report parameter counts, initial/final errors, training/audit residuals and work. Overlay signed heat flux and stress with DVM. Repeat with seed 1730 before claiming a depth advantage.

9. Optimizer — Tables H/J. Compare 120 Adam updates, 40 L-BFGS outer steps and the 100 + 20 hybrid. Verify identical initialization and collocation hashes. Plot component losses against gradient calls and time; include setup, update and diagnostic costs. These budgets are unequal work. Repeat under a closer common work constraint before claiming efficiency.

10. Weights — Tables H/J. Set the energy weight to 0.1, 1 and 10 with density/momentum weights fixed at 1. Report unweighted residuals, the weighted sum, and signed q, σ and Δ profiles/errors. Identify improvements and regressions. Optional zero energy weight is incomplete consistency, not the original BGK problem.

11. Sampling and quadrature — Tables H/I. Compare 32, 64 and 128 collocation points at fixed depth/seed. Then change velocity or characteristic-time quadrature separately, reevaluating the same frozen model to separate integration from fitting. Report DVM spatial/time and velocity sensitivity before attributing a small gain to training.

12. Did the network learn? — Tables H/I. Quantify initial-to-trained changes in all nine fields and independent physics-audit residuals. Explain the small collision fraction at tf/τ = 0.02. Use signed profiles to defend one improvement and one limitation.

blocks.text: Two spatial resolutions at fixed CFL test combined spatial/time sensitivity; minmod prevents assuming a factor-four reduction. Keep failed cases. Disclose any later DVM-based tuning as development use. This short BGK experiment does not establish long-time, stationary or Shakhov performance.
